question: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and a recent myocardial infarction 5 weeks ago is listed for an elective sigmoid colectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Proceed to surgery immediately — delay increases the risk of colonic perforation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elective surgery within 6 weeks of a myocardial infarction carries a prohibitively high reinfarction risk; proceeding immediately is unsafe.

answers.text: Defer elective surgery until at least 6 weeks (ideally 3 months) post-infarction and optimise blood pressure control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Elective surgery is deferred for at least 6 weeks (preferably 3 months) after a myocardial infarction. Optimising blood pressure before theatre is a core preoperative step in risk reduction.

answers.text: Proceed after a single dose of prophylactic aspirin on the morning of surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A single aspirin dose does not mitigate the high cardiac risk. Deferral and cardiac optimisation are required.

answers.text: Obtain a preoperative echocardiogram and proceed to surgery within 48 hours if ejection fraction is >50%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adequate ejection fraction alone does not remove the risk associated with a recent infarction; the 6-week minimum deferral rule applies regardless.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the timing rules for elective surgery after cardiac events and the goals of preoperative optimisation.
Well done. Deferring elective surgery and optimising comorbidities are fundamental principles of preoperative risk management.
